entities.summary:
Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. 310 – c. 395 CE), a preeminent Latin poet and rhetorician, served as a vital intellectual bridge during the tumultuous transition from the classical Roman world to late antiquity. Born in Burdigala (modern Bordeaux) in Roman Gaul, Ausonius rose from a provincial teacher of rhetoric to a powerful figure at the imperial court, ultimately holding the consulship in 379 CE. His life and extensive literary corpus offer an invaluable, firsthand perspective on the social, political, and cultural landscape of the Western Roman Empire during its twilight years, illuminating the enduring vitality of classical learning amidst profound change.

Ausonius's career trajectory began in the educational sphere, where he distinguished himself as a grammarian and rhetorician in his native Bordeaux, attracting students from across Gaul. His fortunes dramatically shifted when Emperor Valentinian I appointed him tutor to his son, the future Emperor Gratian, in 367 CE. This imperial patronage propelled Ausonius to the highest echelons of Roman society, granting him numerous administrative posts, including quaestor sacri palatii (chief legal officer) and praetorian prefect of Gaul. During this period, he composed his most celebrated work, the "Mosella," a vibrant, descriptive poem praising the Moselle River and its surrounding landscape, rich with naturalistic detail and classical allusions. Other significant works include the "Parentalia" and "Commemoratio Professorum Burdigalensium," which provide intimate biographical sketches of his family and fellow teachers, offering unique insights into provincial elite life.
